amendments.rule: A construct noun cannot take the article, so a pointed `בַּ` before one is preposition-only and the English *the* is supplied. Follow MACULA's morphology rather than the pointing. Where the chain's *nomen rectum* does carry an article, that morpheme takes the *the* the ASV writes for the chain even though English fronts it to the phrase's left edge and renders the rectum anarthrously — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone*, `כּוּר הַבַּרְזֶל` → *the furnace of iron*. Supply a *the* on a construct noun only where no article morpheme is present, or for a second English *the* in a multi-level chain, which the article's own leaves for the outer construct: `לְבַב כָּל בְּנֵי הָאָדָם` → *the hearts of all the children of men*. **Fronting is what the anarthrous rendering forces, not a preference for the phrase's left edge.** Where the ASV instead renders the rectum arthrously, writing a *the* before the construct and another before the rectum — `מִשְׁפַּחַת הַקְּהָתִי` → *the families of the Kohathites*, `בְּנֵי הַקְּהָתִי` → *the sons of the Kohathites*, `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city*, `מִשְׁפְּחוֹת הַלֵּוִי` → *the families of the Levites* — nothing is fronted: the article takes the *the* standing before its own word and the construct takes a supplied one, exactly as an outer construct does in a multi-level chain. Count the ASV's *the*s and read which word each stands before, as rule 47 reads which word its single *the* stands before. **And a rectum the ASV renders indefinitely is not an anarthrous one.** Where the article morpheme stands on the rectum, the ASV writes an indefinite article before the rectum's own word, and the phrase's single *the* stands before the construct — `נֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם` → *the body of a man* — nothing is fronted: the *a* is that noun's own under rule 15, one word is not determined twice, and the article is `unrepresented` under this rule's last sentence while the construct takes a supplied *the*. What forces fronting is a rectum the ASV leaves with no determiner at all, as `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* is, so read which determiner stands before the rectum's word before counting the phrase's *the*s. **A construct relation the ASV recasts as an English possessive is not a fronting either.** Where the ASV writes the rectum as a possessive standing before its head noun — `מִלַּת מַלְכָּא` → *the king's matter*, `שַׁלִּיטָא דִּי מַלְכָּא` → *the king's captain*, `שַׁעַר הַמֶּלֶךְ` → *the king's gate* — the *the* at the phrase's left edge stands before the possessor's own word, because an English possessive expression takes the determiner of the possessor and not of the head noun. So the article on the rectum takes it and the construct noun keeps only its own word, a present article morpheme taking its English before a supplied one does; supply a *the* on the construct only where the ASV writes a second one, as `רַב טַבָּחַיָּא דִּי מַלְכָּא` → *the captain of the king's guard* does. Do not read the left edge as evidence of fronting: what fronting answers to is an anarthrous rectum, and here the rectum is the very word the *the* determines. **Read that as the determiner of the possessive, not as the word *the*, and read it whether or not the possessor carries an article of its own.** An English possessive expression takes the determiner of the possessor whatever that determiner is, so an indefinite *a* standing at the phrase's left edge stands before the possessor's word exactly as a *the* does, and where the possessor's word carries no article morpheme the determiner the ASV supplies still goes to that word rather than to the construct noun: `נְשִׂיא בֵית־אָב` → *a prince of* ***a fathers*** *house* gives *a fathers* to `אָב` and *of ... house* to `בַּיִת`, discontinuous around the possessive under rule 25. This is rule 15's supplied determiner placed by this rule's own reasoning — the noun that licenses an English *a* in such a phrase is the possessor, since *a father's house* is the house of *a* father — and the construct noun takes a determiner of its own only where the ASV writes a second one, on the terms just given. A `דִּי` or other relational morpheme standing between the two nouns is rendered inside the possessive and shares the rectum's unit under rule 30. **A rectum that is a proper name is not an exception.** An article MACULA segments off a toponym takes the ASV's *the* on the same terms as one on a common noun, and is never set aside as lexicalized in the name: `בְּנֵי הָרָמָה` → *The children of Ramah* and `אַנְשֵׁי בֵית אֵל וְהָעָי` → *The men of Beth el and Ai* give the single written *the* to the article and leave the construct noun bare. **But an article the ASV spells into its name is already rendered.** Where the rectum is transliterated with its article — `בְּנֵי הַסֹּפֶרֶת` → *the children of Hassophereth* — the article shares the name's unit under rule 30, it has taken its *the* inside that English word rather than as a separate one, and the *the* the ASV does write stands before the construct as a supplied one. Read the transliteration before counting: nothing is fronted from an article English has already spelled out. Mark the article `unrepresented` only where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase at all, as in `הֶעָרִים הָאֵלֶּה` → *these cities*.
amendments.why: NUM.19.13 renders `בְּנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם` as *the body of a man*: the article stands on the rectum, but the ASV writes the rectum indefinite and puts the phrase's only *the* before the construct. Read literally, rule 29's fronting sentence could be taken to cover it, which would give the article a fronted *the* while rule 15 gives `אָדָם` its own *a* — determining one word twice with contradictory determiners. The rule's own counting sentence does not settle it either, because fronting is precisely the case where position is overridden. The inserted paragraph closes that gap on the rule's existing reasoning, and it is the same reasoning the possessive paragraph already applies when it sends an indefinite *a* to the possessor's word rather than to the construct. It is a narrowing of the fronting sentence, not a new licence: the chapter is aligned this way at 19.13 while 19.16 and 19.21 front normally over anarthrous recta, and nothing in the corpus dump for `הַ` contradicts either reading.

conventions: mey (ha)niddah is aligned as a construct chain in all five places: niddah takes the relation the ASV recasts as for impurity (rule 19), and the phrase's single the goes to the article morpheme where one stands and the rectum is rendered anarthrously (19.21, twice), and to the construct as a supplied determiner where no article morpheme is in the chain (19.13, 19.20). 19.9's for a water for impurity gives the indefinite article to the construct noun under rule 15 and writes a for for each preposition.

tame hu' is aligned by what the ASV writes for the pronoun and not by the shared Hebrew: 19.20 writes he is unclean, so hu' takes he and the copula joins the predicate adjective; 19.15 writes only is unclean after the long fronted subject every open vessel which..., so the resuming hu' is the unrendered occurrence and is unrepresented (rules 20, 22). BSB represents the 19.15 pronoun; that is its convention, not an error here. Do not harmonise the two.

Every English object pronoun the ASV supplies where no object morpheme stands in the clause is its own added unit and is never folded into the verb beside it: cast it (19.6), lay them up (19.9), dip it and sprinkle it (19.18), toucheth it (19.22). Where an object marker or a suffix is present the pronoun goes to that morpheme instead (19.3, 19.5, 19.19). The cross-verse candidate table is blind to added units, so this is the chapter's only record that they were checked against each other.

report: Checked all 51 candidate lemma groups. Every multi-treatment bucket is the ASV writing different English for the same Hebrew, and each difference is licensed by what is written: the substantival article's supplied pronoun (he that / He that / one that / him that, 19.8, 19.10, 19.11, 19.14, 19.18, 19.21) against the attributive article rendered by a relative (19.10, 19.22) and against a plain written the (19.18); waw as and / And / But / Then / then / that, and unrendered where the ASV opens the apodosis bare (19.11, 19.20); kol fused with a following article or asher into one word (Whosoever 19.13, whosoever 19.16, whatsoever 19.22) against the same pairs written as two words (every one that, twice in 19.14), which is rule 30's one-English-word condition doing its work.

Article counting in construct chains is consistent chapter-wide and follows rule 29 by which word each the stands before: arthrous rendering, each morpheme takes its own (19.2, 19.9, 19.10); anarthrous rectum, the article's the is fronted (19.16 the open field, 19.21 twice the water for impurity); no article morpheme in the chain, the construct takes a supplied the (19.4, 19.6, 19.13, 19.17, 19.20). The one apparent exception, 19.13's the body of a man, is licensed rather than a split: the ASV renders the rectum indefinite, so the a is that noun's under rule 15 and no the was written for the article. Rule 29 did not cover an indefinitely rendered rectum, and that gap is returned below as an amendment.

The candidate table is keyed by source lemma and cannot see added units, so I read the dump end to end for them. Six: five supplied object pronouns in clauses with no object morpheme (cast it 19.6, lay them up 19.9, dip it and sprinkle it 19.18, toucheth it 19.22) and one supplied coordinator (19.2, opening the second relative clause). No verse folds such a pronoun into the verb beside it, and every clause that does write a marker or a suffix gives the pronoun to that morpheme (19.3, 19.5, 19.19). Recorded as a convention, since nothing mechanical checks it.

Same-Hebrew-different-English pairs I checked individually and left alone: hayah le- with its lamed rendered for in 19.10 but unrepresented in 19.9 and 19.21, where the ASV writes no preposition; tame hu' with the pronoun written in 19.20 and not in 19.15; chuqqat olam as for a statute for ever (19.10, rule 19) and as a perpetual statute (19.21, rule 28); ish tahor as a man that is clean (19.9) and a clean person (19.18); the article on erev aligned in 19.7, 19.8 and 19.10 and unrepresented in 19.19, 19.21 and 19.22. In each the ASV, not the source, differs.

Fusion decisions are internally consistent: min-chuts to without with the following lamed unrepresented (19.3, 19.9), be-tokh to among (19.10) against min-tokh split as from the midst (19.20), bo to therewith (19.12) and alayw to thereto (19.17) against upon him written in two words (19.13, 19.20), and le-panayw split as before his face (19.3). All turn on rule 30's one-rendering condition, and each verse says so in its note.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The 36 recurring R, Rd and Td tokens are the documented function-morpheme convention difference, and they are the bets of nagac be- left unrepresented under rule 40 (fourteen of them, 19.11 through 19.22, uniformly, while their assimilated articles still take the written the in 19.18), the lamed of le'mor under rule 27, and articles the ASV writes anarthrously. The named singletons are rule 16 object markers (19.8, 19.13), rule 22 resumptive morphemes (19.2, 19.15, 19.22) and the two unrendered apodosis waws (19.11, 19.20). I made no edge change to improve the rate.
No patches. The chapter's 558 units partition cleanly and I found no construction analysed two ways with nothing in the source or the ASV to license the difference.
